t: Introduction: when an examination is ordered
n: This topic is devoted to the forensic medical examination of the bodies of foetuses and newborn infants. First, let us consider when an examination is ordered. The examination is carried out when there are signs of violent death or suspicion of it. First case: the body of an infant whose mother is unknown has been found. Second case: stillbirth in delivery outside a medical institution. Third case: a complaint about the medical care given to a pregnant woman.

Now the questions put to the examination. Six special questions are put to the examination. Unlike other examinations of bodies, these questions have a special character. They fall into four groups. Period and life: whether the infant is newborn and whether it was born alive. Development: what the gestational age is and whether it is viable. Duration and care: how long it lived and whether there was care. In addition, general questions are asked: cause of death, its age, injuries and the mechanism of their infliction.

t: Newborn status: comparison in three sciences
n: The concept of the newborn is interpreted differently in three sciences. In forensic medicine this concept differs from that in paediatrics and obstetrics. In paediatrics this period is 4 weeks, in obstetrics and gynaecology 7 days, and in forensic medicine 24 hours. This concept is also connected with criminal law. According to Article 99 of the Criminal Code, if a mother kills her child during delivery, the penalty is milder. Note: Article 97 relates to killing by another person, and Article 99 to killing by the mother. The penalty differs in these two articles.

In forensic medicine, the newborn period is the first 24 hours after delivery. This period is closely connected with legislative requirements. Article 99 of the Criminal Code separately identifies the deliberate killing by a mother of her child during delivery or immediately after birth. The penalty is considerably milder than for deliberate homicide. Labour lasts roughly about a day. Because of pain and her psycho-emotional state, the mother may injure her child without fully realising it. Remember: if another person commits such an act, it is assessed under Article 97 of the Criminal Code, that is, as deliberate homicide. Article 99 and Article 97 are not the same.

t: Case analysis: the concept of the newborn
n: Now a case analysis. The body of an infant whose mother is unknown has been found. The umbilical cord is not separated from the body and placenta. In such a case a forensic medical examination is ordered. First question: is the infant newborn? In paediatrics this period is 4 weeks, that is, the neonatal period; in obstetrics 7 days; and in forensic medicine the first 24 hours. An umbilical cord not separated from the body and placenta is regarded as an absolute, that is, entirely reliable sign of being newborn. The other signs are relative: they may also be found on the second and subsequent days of life. Therefore the expert assesses the signs together.

In the absence of external injury, traces of blood on the body are a sign of being newborn. They are formed by tearing of the soft tissues of the birth canal. After the infant's body is washed, the blood traces disappear. Therefore the absence of this sign on a washed body does not exclude being newborn. Vernix caseosa is a whitish-grey semi-liquid mass consisting of a mixture of sebaceous gland secretion, desquamated epidermal cells, lanugo hair and amniotic fluid. In the uterus it protects the skin from maceration by amniotic fluid. It is most abundant in the folds, the axillae and the perineum; if not washed off, it persists for up to a week.

t: Caput succedaneum and cephalohaematoma: the difference
n: Now let us compare two conditions: caput succedaneum and cephalohaematoma. In caput succedaneum the soft tissues swell because of compression in the pelvis; the cause is compression in the pelvic ring, and inside there is blood-stained serous fluid. It also occurs in the projection of the sutures and resolves in 2–3 days. In cephalohaematoma, by contrast, blood is effused under the periosteum; the cause is birth trauma. It lies on the bone and extends to the sutures, and resolves in 2 weeks or more. Attention: risk of error. The swelling also occurs in the projection of the sutures, whereas a cephalohaematoma is limited by the sutures.

Meconium is the first stool. It is a dark green or brownish-green, semi-liquid, uniform mass. Meconium is found in the large intestine, around the anus, and in the buttock and thigh regions. Its composition includes mucus, bile pigments, desquamated intestinal epithelium, amniotic fluid and lanugo hair. The composition varies with the duration of pregnancy. It is usually passed completely from the intestine within 1–2 days after delivery. In premature infants this period extends to 3–4 days.

t: Changes of the umbilical cord: timeline
n: Let us look at changes of the umbilical cord along a timeline. A fresh cord is moist, shiny, whitish-reddish. On drying it shrivels and takes on a brownish-yellow tint. In live birth, a reddish demarcation ring appears at its base after several hours; this is a sign of reactive inflammation. Then the cord becomes brownish-black, and on days 5–7 it falls off along the ring. The absence of the ring or its initial sign, as well as an unseparated cord, is an absolute, that is, entirely reliable sign.

Now absolute and relative signs. Three signs are regarded as absolute, that is, entirely reliable: primary atelectasis of the lungs, the absence or initial state of the demarcation ring, and an unseparated umbilical cord. The remaining signs are relative: blood traces, vernix caseosa, caput succedaneum and meconium. Relative signs may also be found on the second and subsequent days of the infant's life. Attention: vernix caseosa is not an absolute sign, because if it is not washed off, it persists for up to a week.

t: Quick question: signs of being newborn
n: Let us consolidate our knowledge with quick questions. Which three signs are absolute? Primary atelectasis, absence or initial sign of the demarcation ring, an unseparated cord. When is meconium passed completely? Usually in 1–2 days, extending to 3–4 days in premature infants. When do caput succedaneum and cephalohaematoma resolve? The swelling in 2–3 days, the cephalohaematoma in 2 weeks or more. For memorising, the mnemonic "L-D-C": Lung atelectasis, Demarcation ring, Cord. This is a brief memory aid compiled for teaching.

t: Case analysis: signs of being newborn
n: Case analysis. On the body of the infant found there is whitish-grey vernix caseosa, and meconium is visible near the anus. The umbilical cord is not separated from the body and placenta, and is not cut. Question: which sign is entirely reliable? Answer: the unseparated cord. The vernix and meconium are relative signs. Vernix on an unwashed body persists for up to a week. Therefore being newborn cannot be proved by them alone.

We turn to the criteria of live birth. According to WHO criteria, an infant outside the mother's body must have breathing, a heartbeat, umbilical cord pulsation or voluntary movement. In forensic medicine, methods of detecting a heartbeat, cord pulsation and voluntary movement after death have not yet been developed. Therefore the question of live birth is decided mainly by establishing whether the infant breathed or not. Live birth is determined from the results of various tests and of macroscopic, microscopic and laboratory examinations.

The lung test is associated with the names of Galen, Rauger and Schreyer. The test was first applied in 1681 by I. Schreyer. A lung that has not breathed is heavier than water, with a specific gravity of 1.05–1.06. In a lung that has breathed, owing to air, the specific gravity decreases and falls below 1.0. The procedure is as follows: first ligatures are placed on the trachea and oesophagus, then the organ complex is placed in a vessel of water. If it sinks, the separate lungs are tested, then lobes and pieces. If it floats, the test is finished. At the stage at which a positive result is obtained, the test is stopped.

t: False results of the lung test
n: False results are possible in the lung test. A false positive result occurs in putrefaction, because putrefactive gases lift the lung. A false positive also occurs after artificial respiration, in which case the pieces behave unequally in water. A false positive is also possible in freezing; an unthawed lung floats, and once thawed it sinks. A false negative result is found in secondary atelectasis, that is, in a lung that first breathed and then underwent atelectasis. If pieces that have floated because of putrefactive gas are squeezed by hand under water, they do not float up again. In a false negative, Taranukhin's method (1907) or Trakhtenberg's modification (1958) is used. Attention: flotation of the lung does not always mean that the infant breathed.

In secondary atelectasis, a lung that has breathed undergoes atelectasis because of inflammation or obstruction of the airways. The ordinary lung test may then give a false negative. In such a case Taranukhin's method (1907) or its Trakhtenberg modification (1958) is recommended. A piece of lung is placed in a flask of water, then air is drawn out, creating a reduced pressure in the flask. If a piece that sank at ordinary pressure floats to the surface of the water at reduced pressure, there is air remaining in it. This indicates secondary atelectasis.

We shall look at two more tests. The Breslau test (1865) is based on the fact that in breathing part of the air passes through the oesophagus into the stomach and intestines. Ligatures are placed on the stomach and intestines, and they are put in a vessel of water. Air-filled parts float up, and when pierced air bubbles are seen. On a putrefied body and with artificial ventilation of the lungs this test gives a false positive, so it is not recommended. The radiological test (Dillon, 1939) cannot distinguish a lung that has breathed from artificial ventilation and putrefactive gases. It needs special equipment and is not used at present.

t: Macroscopic signs: born alive and stillborn
n: Now macroscopic signs: the lungs of an infant born alive and of a stillborn one. A lung that has breathed almost fills the thoracic cavity, is elastic, and has an uneven surface. A lung that has not breathed is small in volume, denser, closer to the spine, with a relatively smooth surface. On compression, frothy blood is released from a lung that has breathed, and less blood from one that has not. In live birth the chest is barrel-shaped, the diaphragm is at the level of the 6th–7th rib, the lung is marbled, and weighs 85–90 g. In stillbirth the chest is flat, the diaphragm is at the level of the 4th–5th rib, the lung is uniformly bluish-dark red, and weighs 55–60 g.

Let us look at microscopic signs. The elastic fibres are arranged in bundles in a lung that has not breathed, and in regular order in one that has. In a lung that has not breathed the alveoli are not expanded, the epithelium is cuboidal, the septum is thick, and there is no blood in the capillaries. In a lung that has breathed the alveoli are expanded, the epithelium is flat, the septum is thinned, and the capillaries are congested. Hyaline membranes consist of blood proteins, that is, albumin, globulin and fibrin. In a lung that has not breathed they are absent. In stillborns, "bud-like" and "cushion-like" protrusions are present inside the pulmonary arteries.

Quick questions on the tests. Who first applied the lung test in forensic medicine, and when? I. Schreyer, in 1681. With whose name is the gastrointestinal test associated? V. Breslau, 1865. When does the lung test give a false positive? In putrefaction, after artificial respiration, and in a poorly thawed frozen lung. When does a false negative result occur? In secondary atelectasis; in this case Taranukhin's method (1907) is used.

Case analysis. The infant's body is putrefied, and the lung complex floated to the surface of the water. Can one conclude that it was born alive? Putrefactive gases give a false positive. If the parts do not float up again when squeezed by hand under water, the cause is putrefactive gas. In putrefaction the gastrointestinal test also gives a false positive, so it is not recommended. In addition, on microscopy the expansion of the alveoli and the flat epithelium are assessed. Flotation alone is not sufficient for a conclusion.

t: Concepts of full term and maturity
n: The concepts of full term and maturity. Full term is a set of signs showing that pregnancy lasted on average 10 lunar months, or 280 days. According to the World Health Organization, that is, the WHO, delivery at 37–42 weeks is regarded as timely. An infant born in this period is called full-term. The body length of a full-term infant is on average 50–54 cm and the weight 3000–3500 g. Attention: full term and maturity are not the same. Maturity is development sufficient for life outside the mother's body: length not less than 45 cm, weight not less than 2500 g.

Let us calculate gestational age by formulae. Haase's formula gives gestational age in lunar months. In the first and second halves the method of calculation differs. In the first half, the square root of the body length is taken, for example with 16 cm this gives 4 lunar months. In the second half, the body length is divided by 5, for example with 40 cm this gives 8 lunar months. The Balthazard–Dervieux index is 5.6. If it is multiplied by the body length, the age is obtained in days: for 40 cm, 224 days, that is, 8 months. By I. Yakupov's method (1981), the circumference of the foetal head is divided by 3.4; for example with 34 cm this gives 10 lunar months.

t: Gestational age by the umbilical cord and placenta
n: Gestational age can also be determined by the length of the umbilical cord and the weight of the placenta; this is given in table 10.1. In the abbreviated table, in the 6th month the cord is 38 cm and the placenta 250 g. In the 7th month 42 cm and 340 g. In the 8th month 46 cm and 410 g. In the 10th month 50 cm and 500 g. For the 9th month, not shown in the table, the cord is 47 cm and the placenta weight 470 g. Therefore in the examination, the placenta and cord submitted together with the body are also examined carefully.

t: Ossification centres and the swallowing reflex
n: In determining gestational age, the ossification centres in the bones are examined: the femur, calcaneus and talus. In the calcaneus the centre appears in the 5th month, size 0.8–1.1 cm. In the talus in the 7th month, 0.7–1.0 cm. In the epiphysis of the femur, that is, Béclard's centre, in the 9th month, 0.5–0.7 cm. Diseases in pregnancy, smoking, alcohol and narcotics delay the centres, and sometimes they do not appear at all. The swallowing reflex appears in the 8th month. Lanugo hairs in the meconium are called the Shibkov–Markovin sign.

Case analysis. The body of a foetus has been found, body length 40 cm. Let us calculate the gestational age by Haase's formula. For the second half, the body length is divided by 5: 40 : 5 = 8 lunar months. For the first half, the square root is taken, for example 16 cm is 4 months. To check, we multiply the Balthazard–Dervieux index of 5.6 by the body length: 40 × 5.6 = 224 days, that is, 8 lunar months. Question: is a foetus with a body length of 40 cm regarded as mature? Criterion of maturity: length 45 cm and over, weight at least 2500 g.

Viability is the infant's ability to live outside the mother's body. An infant born alive may also be non-viable. By the WHO criterion, an infant under 25 cm in length and under 500 g in weight is non-viable because of extreme prematurity. In this case the body is not opened; only an external examination is made, and weight and length are measured. Malformations such as anencephaly and a two-chambered heart preclude life. Birth trauma, that is, crushing of the brain and fractures of the cervical vertebrae, likewise. If an external malformation is found, for example a sixth finger or cleft lip, the brain and internal organs are examined carefully to exclude an internal malformation.

The duration of life is determined by the dynamics of morphological changes. The time periods are approximate, so as many signs as possible are taken into account. The demarcation ring and the passage of meconium are formed by the end of the first day. Hyaline membranes indicate that the infant lived at least 1–2 hours. Secondary atelectasis forms after at least 5–6 hours. If air is only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours. At 5–6 hours air fills the small intestine. Attention: hyaline membranes and secondary atelectasis form at different times.

Whether there was care of the infant is important for the legal assessment of the event in inquiry and investigation. External signs: the infant is swaddled, clothing is on it, and the cord is cut and tied. The body has been cleaned of blood traces and vernix caseosa. On internal examination, milk or a similar mass is found in the stomach. Test yourself: what is the minimum number of hours needed for the formation of hyaline membranes? Name five signs of care.

Case analysis. In the body of a newborn, air is only in the stomach and absent in the large intestine. On the cord there are initial signs of the ring. If air is only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours. Air that has passed into the intestine indicates longer life. The ring signs on the cord correspond to live birth. The time periods are approximate, so the conclusion is not based on a single sign. Question: how long did the infant live, and was there care? For care, check the swaddling, clothing, cord, cleanliness of the body and milk in the stomach.

t: Causes of death: antenatal and intranatal periods
n: Now the causes of death: the antenatal and intranatal periods. In antenatal death the main cause is intrauterine asphyxia; the placenta and cord are also examined. Signs: signs of rapid death, aspiration of fluid, much meconium; the lumen of the large intestine is narrowed. Haemorrhages into the meninges and ventricles are possible, often symmetrical. The causes fall into groups. Placenta and cord: placenta praevia, infarct, knot in the cord. Maternal disease: syphilis, viral infection, heart defect, toxicosis. Birth trauma: fractures of the skull bones and intracranial haemorrhages. With a narrow pelvis and a large foetus, the head remains compressed for a long time.

Signs of birth trauma. With a narrow pelvis, a large foetus or weak labour, the head is compressed for a long time, the bones of the cranial vault break, and haemorrhage occurs into the cranial cavity. The parietal and frontal bones are more often injured; radial and depressed fractures are found. Haemorrhage into the meninges and brain substance; especially severe if the tentorium cerebelli or falx is torn. Attention: in birth trauma there is no external injury or wound. If a woman helped with her hand, abrasions, bruises and a tear of the corner of the mouth occur on the face and neck.

t: Violent death: active and passive infanticide
n: Violent death occurs mainly in the postnatal period; in the antenatal and intranatal periods it is very rare. For law enforcement it is important to state not whether it is active or passive, but the exact cause of death. Antenatal violent death is connected with inflicting mechanical injury on the pregnant woman or poisoning her. In active killing, definite actions are done to the infant: strangulation, closing the respiratory openings, and also drowning, compression, throwing into fire. In passive killing, the infant is left without care: external bleeding if the cord is not tied, and also chilling and starvation.

Case analysis. The body of a newborn has no external injury, but intracranial haemorrhage has been found. In birth trauma, haemorrhage occurs into the meninges and brain substance, but no external injury, including a wound, is formed. Attention: if the mother, helping herself, injures the infant with her hand, abrasions, bruises and a tear of the corner of the mouth occur on the face and neck. Question: if with a narrow pelvis, a large foetus and weak labour the head is compressed for a long time, what changes appear in the skull bones and inside the skull?

t: Features of the examination: stages of investigation
n: Let us consider the stages of the expert examination. The first stage is external examination: length, weight, dimensions of the head and chest, blood traces, vernix caseosa, meconium and malformations are studied. In the second stage the placenta, that is, its weight and shape, and the cord, that is, its length, moisture and knot, are examined carefully. The third stage is internal examination: the chest and abdominal cavities. The incision begins from the lower lip, and before reaching the umbilicus turns aside. In the fourth stage windows are opened in the skull. The last stage is laboratory: histological and forensic biological examinations.

t: What is studied in the external examination
n: What is studied in the external examination. The articles submitted with the body, the swaddling and the clothing are studied; anthropometric measurements are carried out. The body length, weight, head dimensions, that is, circumference, large, small, oblique, straight and biparietal, and also chest and shoulder circumference, are measured. Attention is paid to blood traces, vernix caseosa, caput succedaneum, fontanelles, skin colour, firmness of the ear and nasal cartilages, and the state of the genitalia. The length of the nails, contamination with meconium, external malformations and ossification centres, that is, of the femur, calcaneus and talus, are examined.

The internal examination begins with the chest and abdominal cavities. The main incision is made not from the chin but from the lower lip. So as not to damage the integrity of the umbilical vessels, the incision, before reaching the umbilicus, is continued towards the pubic ligaments. In the cranial cavity, so that the falx and tentorium cerebelli remain intact, the bones are cut with scissors and windows are opened in the frontal, parietal and temporal bones. Laboratory materials: internal organs, pieces of placenta and cord for histological examination, and forensic biological examination to determine the blood group.

Causes of non-violent death by period. In the antenatal period the causes are diseases of the pregnant woman, that is, respiratory viral infection, syphilis, heart defect, toxicosis of pregnancy, and malformations of the foetus; the main event is intrauterine asphyxia. In the intranatal period the main cause is birth trauma: with a narrow pelvis, a large foetus or weak labour, the head is compressed for a long time and the skull bones break. If during delivery the mother helps with her hand, abrasions, bruises and tears of the corners of the mouth are possible in the foetal face and neck. In the postnatal period the causes are extreme prematurity, disproportionate malformations, haemolytic disease, congenital toxoplasmosis and pneumopathies.

Intrauterine asphyxia and cerebral haemorrhage. The lumen of the large intestine of a full-term foetus is usually wide, up to several centimetres, and filled with meconium. In intrauterine asphyxia, the meconium is passed completely or partially from the intestine, and the lumen of the large intestine is considerably narrowed. Haemorrhages into the meninges and ventricles may be observed; they are often symmetrical. Antenatal violent death is considerably rarer: it is connected mainly with inflicting mechanical injury on the pregnant woman or poisoning her.

Let us sum up. In forensic medicine, the newborn period is the first 24 hours. Live birth is decided mainly by whether the infant breathed. Gestational age is determined by anthropometry and signs. An infant under 25 cm in length and under 500 g in weight is regarded as non-viable. Death is non-violent, that is, ante-, intra- and postnatal, or violent, mainly postnatal. The main thing is to state the exact cause of death. For revision, repeat: the questions of the examination, the difference and signs of being newborn, the absolute signs, the lung test and secondary atelectasis.
